summary: IPFIX is a standard way for devices to export information about network traffic flows. This RFC defines SNMP managed objects for monitoring IPFIX Exporters and Collectors, including basic configuration information.

plainLanguage.summary:
IPFIX is a way for a router to report the traffic it sees to a collector elsewhere. This RFC is about looking inside that arrangement from the management system.

It defines SNMP tables that answer questions such as: which collectors does this exporter send to, over which protocol and port, which record layouts has it sent, what is counted at each observation point, and how much data has moved. A second module holds the standard ways of filtering and sampling the traffic before it is reported.

subtitle: The SNMP tables a router or collector exposes so operators can see how its IPFIX flow export is configured and performing.

tldr.problem: IPFIX lets a router report the traffic flows it observes to a collector, but an operator had no standard way to ask the router or the collector, over SNMP, what that export was doing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two MIB modules. The IPFIX MIB exposes seven tables describing transport sessions, templates, exports, metering processes, observation points and selection processes, plus statistical counters for them. The IPFIX SELECTOR MIB provides a place to register filtering and sampling functions.
tldr.outcome: An operator can read which collectors an exporter talks to, which templates it sends, how it fails over, and how much data it has moved. The RFC obsoletes RFC 5815.

today: RFC 6615 is a Proposed Standard from June 2012. It obsoletes RFC 5815 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It removes the IPFIX SELECTOR MIB registry defined in the earlier document and replaces it with a sub-registry of the SMI Numbers registry.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document defines two MIB modules for monitoring IP Flow Information eXport devices, including Exporters and Collectors. While most of the objects defined by the IPFIX MIB module must be implemented, some objects may be implemented corresponding to the functionality implemented in the equipment.

Since the IPFIX architecture foresees the possibility of using Filtering and/or Sampling functions to reduce the data volume, this document also provides the IPFIX SELECTOR MIB module, which contains the standardized selection methods and is controlled by IANA. The full configuration of the IPFIX Metering Process is out of the scope of these MIB modules.
sections.plainLanguage: Two modules, then. One describes the parts of an IPFIX deployment that an operator needs to see. The other is a place where new ways of selecting which packets to report can be registered.

sections.title: The IPFIX Documents It Builds On
sections.content:
The IPFIX protocol provides network administrators with access to IP Flow information. The architecture for the export of measured IP Flow information out of an IPFIX Exporting Process to a Collecting Process is defined in RFC 5470, per the requirements defined in RFC 3917. The protocol document RFC 5101 specifies how IPFIX Data Records and Templates are carried via a congestion-aware transport protocol from Exporting Processes to Collecting Processes. IPFIX has a formal description of IPFIX Information Elements, their name, type and additional semantic information, as specified in RFC 5102. Finally, RFC 5472 describes what type of applications can use the IPFIX protocol and how they can use the information provided, and how the IPFIX framework relates to other architectures and frameworks.

It is assumed that flow metering, export and collection are performed according to the IPFIX architecture defined in RFC 5470, and that the monitored configuration parameters of the export and collection of Flow Templates and Data Records are modelled according to RFC 5101.

Packet selection methods that may be optionally used by the IPFIX Metering Process are not considered in this MIB document. They are defined in the Packet Sampling framework and Sampling techniques documents. Nevertheless, the basis for defining Sampling and Filtering functions is given with the IPFIX SELECTOR MIB module. Since the PSAMP export protocol is based on the IPFIX protocol, the Sampling and Filtering functions can be added to the IPFIX SELECTOR MIB module as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: IPFIX itself is split across several documents: one for the architecture, one for the protocol on the wire, one that lists every measurement that can be reported, and one about who uses it. This RFC only adds the management view on top.

sections.title: The Tables of the IPFIX MIB
sections.content:
The IPFIX MIB module consists of seven main tables: the Transport Session table, the Template table and the corresponding Template Definition table, the Export table, the Metering Process table, the Observation Point table and the Selection Process table. Since the IPFIX architecture foresees the possibility of using Filtering and/or Sampling functions to reduce the data volume, the module provides the basic objects for these functions with the Selection Process table, and the IPFIX SELECTOR MIB module provides the standard Filtering and Sampling functions that can be referenced in it. All remaining objects contain statistical values for the different tables in the module.

The Transport Session table is the basis of the module. It holds every transport session between the Exporter and the Collector, and says which transport protocol each one uses. For UDP and TCP it also carries the source and destination addresses and ports. For SCTP it carries the index of the SCTP association in the SCTP MIB module. An object says whether the device is collecting or exporting on that session, and the table also holds the configured refresh parameters for Templates and Options Templates used across unreliable connections such as UDP, the IPFIX version in use and a status for the session.

The Template table lists all Templates and Options Templates that are sent by an Exporter or received by a Collector. They are unique per Observation Domain and per Transport Session, so the table is indexed by the Transport Session index and the Observation Domain ID, and it holds the Set ID and the time the template was last sent or received.

The Template Definition table lists all the Information Elements contained in a Template or Options Template. It has the same indexes as the Template table plus the Template ID, and its own index denotes the order of the Information Element inside the Template. Besides the Information Element ID and the length of the encoded value, it carries the enterprise number for enterprise-specific Information Elements and flags for each element, indicating whether it is used for scoping or as a Flow Key.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables mirror how IPFIX actually works. A transport session is one connection to one collector. A template is the layout of a record. A template definition lists the measurements in that layout, in order. The remaining tables cover where the traffic is watched, how the records are cached, which collector the records go to, and which packets get selected.

sections.title: The Export Table and Transport Session Groups
sections.content:
On Exporters, the Export table can be used to support features like failover, load-balancing and duplicate export to several Collectors. It has three indexes that link an entry with the Metering Process table and with the Transport Session table. Entries with the same export index and the same metering process cache ID define a Transport Session group, and a member type for each group member describes its functionality. All Transport Sessions referenced in this table must have a device mode value of exporting.

If the Exporter does not use Transport Session grouping, then each export index contains a single metering process cache ID, and thus a single Transport Session; this session must have a member type value of primary. For failover, a Transport Session group can contain one Transport Session with member type primary and several Transport Sessions with type secondary. For load-balancing or parallel export, all Transport Sessions in the group must have the same member type, either loadBalancing or parallel. The algorithms used for failover or load-balancing are out of the scope of this document.

The RFC walks through the steps a manager needs to understand what the backups are for Template Records exported from a specific Exporter to a specific Collector: look up the Collector address in the Transport Session table, double-check the Exporter address in the same row, note the Transport Session index, use that index in the Template table to find the pairs of Observation Domain ID and Template ID, then reuse the same index in the Export table to find the entry whose member type is primary, note its export index, and under the same three index values look up the entries whose member type is different from primary to find the backup Transport Session.
sections.plainLanguage: This table says which connection is the main one and which are the spares. An exporter can send the same records to a second collector, and this table is how a manager finds out that it is doing so.

sections.title: Metering Processes and Observation Points
sections.content:
The Metering Process consists of a set of functions. Maintaining the Flow Records is one of them, responsible for passing the Flow Records to the Exporting Process and for detecting flow expiration. The Flow Records maintained by the Metering Process can be grouped by the Observation Points at which they are observed, and the instance that maintains such a group is a kind of cache. For this reason the Metering Process table is indexed by cache IDs. Each cache can be maintained by a separate instance of the Metering Process, and an object may reference an Observation Point group from the Observation Point table. If no Observation Point is specified for the Flow Records, that reference must be zero. The active and idle timeouts specify when flows are expired.

The Observation Point table groups Observation Points with a group ID. Each entry contains the Observation Domain ID in which the Observation Point is located, and a reference to the ENTITY MIB module or the Interfaces MIB module. At least one of those two references must exist for a valid Observation Point entry; if a reference is given in both, both must point to the same physical interface, and if one cannot be given its reference must be zero. A direction can also be given, to say more specifically which flow to monitor.

The Selection Process table supports the usage of Filtering and Sampling functions. It contains lists of functions per Metering Process cache. The selection process index forms groups of selection methods applied to an observed packet stream, and the selector index gives the order in which the functions are applied to the packets observed at the Observation Points associated with the cache: methods with a lower selector index are applied first. The functions are referenced by object identifiers pointing to each function with its parameters. If no Filtering or Sampling function is used for a Metering Process, an entry for the Metering Process should be created that points to the Select All function.
sections.plainLanguage: A metering process is the part of the router that measures traffic and holds the records until they are exported; the table says which observation points feed it and how long a record may sit there. The selection process table says which filtering and sampling functions run over the packets, and in what order.

sections.title: The IPFIX SELECTOR MIB
sections.content:
The IPFIX SELECTOR MIB module provides the standard Filtering and Sampling functions that can be referenced in the Selection Process table. All standard Filtering and Sampling functions must be registered in the subtree under the ipfixSelectorFunctions object, whose top-level object identifiers must be registered in a sub-registry maintained by IANA. The first entry in this subtree is the Select All function, defined as the first child of ipfixSelectorFunctions.

New Selector Functions must be registered at IANA and are subject to Expert Review. The group of experts must check the requested MIB objects for completeness and accuracy of the description, and requests that duplicate the functionality of existing objects should be declined. The smallest available object identifier should be assigned to new objects, and the specification of new objects should follow the structure in the RFC and must be published using a well-established and persistent publication medium.

The structure every selection method should follow is a subtree introduced by an object named ipfixFunc followed by the function name, with the objects in the subtree prefixed by that name. The subtree contains an object named ipfixFunc followed by the function name and Avail, of type TruthValue, saying whether the function is available. If the method takes parameters, the MIB should contain a table named ipfixFunc followed by the function name and Parameters, holding all the parameters the method specifies; an entry in that table is referenced by the IPFIX MIB module when the method with parameters is used. The example in the RFC shows a function MyFunc with three integer parameters, holding two instances of parameter sets, and a Selection Process table that applies the same function twice with different parameter sets.
sections.plainLanguage: New ways of choosing which packets to report are registered in a fixed place, each one as a small branch of the management tree. The rule is simple: one object saying whether the function exists, and, if it takes settings, one table holding those settings.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There are no management objects defined in this MIB module that have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write and/or read-create. So, if this MIB module is implemented correctly, there is no risk that an intruder can alter or create any management objects of this module via direct SNMP SET operations.

Some of the readable objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. The Transport Session table and the Export table contain configuration data that may reveal information about the network infrastructure. The Metering Process table and the Observation Point table contain configuration data that may reveal information about the IPFIX device itself and the network infrastructure. The ipfixSelectorFunctions subtree currently contains no sensitive data but might want to be secured anyway, since it may contain sensitive data in a future version. All other objects and tables contain no data considered sensitive.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. Even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPsec, there is no control as to who on the secure network is allowed to access and read the objects in this module. Implementations must provide the security features described by the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for authentication and privacy via the User-based Security Model with the AES cipher algorithm, and may also provide support for the Transport Security Model in combination with a secure transport such as SSH or TLS. Deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is not recommended; instead it is recommended to deploy SNMPv3 and enable cryptographic security. It is then the operator's responsibility to configure the SNMP entity so that the objects are reachable only by principals with legitimate rights.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing in this module can be changed over SNMP, so there is nothing to break by writing to it. The tables do reveal how the network is wired, so reading them should be restricted, and the RFC asks for SNMPv3 with encryption.
